title: User Execution: Malicious Library
summary: Malicious library is the sub-technique where execution happens because a user or a build pipeline installs a software package that is hostile. The parent technique covers user driven execution generally; here the payload arrives inside a dependency. The observed patterns are consistent: a brand new package that copies the name of a popular one with a small spelling change, a package name that imitates a private internal package in the hope of a dependency confusion pull, a legitimate well used library that has been taken over or backdoored upstream, and a package whose install time script, post install hook, or imported module performs the malicious work the first time it is used. Because installation usually runs in a development, build or automation context, the resulting process tree is ordinary for that environment, which is why detection leans on context rather than on a single process: a network client spawned by the package manager, build agents reaching hosts that are not source control or registries, newly published dependencies appearing in a lock file, packages without repository history or maintainer background, and a build step that suddenly runs an unexpected binary or script. Supply chain protections such as pinned versions, internal registry mirrors, provenance checks and review of new dependencies are the structural defences.

beginner.definition: This means the attacker hides bad code inside a software package. Developers install packages to save time, so this is a normal habit. The name may be almost the same as a popular one. Installing it runs the attacker's code on your computer or build server.
beginner.whyItMatters: Modern software is built from hundreds of outside packages, and each one is trusted. A single bad package may reach every system that builds your product. Some packages run code during installation, before anyone reviews anything. If a build server is hit, the attacker can change what you ship.
howItWorks: The attacker uploads a package to a public library, or takes over an existing package.
The name is chosen to look like a popular package, with a small spelling difference.
A developer or an automated build installs it, often as a dependency of something else.
During installation, or on first use, the package runs its hidden code.
That code steals credentials, sets up persistence, or starts mining on the build server.
Because the build server is trusted, the attacker may also alter the software it produces.
beginner.example: Picture a shared flat where everyone borrows tools from a labelled shelf. Someone puts a drill in a case with almost the same label as the real one. A flatmate grabs it, and it works at first, then quietly copies the front door key. The shelf looked orderly, and the label was the disguise.
takeaways: Check new dependencies before adding them, and prefer packages with real history and maintainers.
Watch for build systems or package managers making network connections they never made before.
Pin versions and use internal mirrors so an unexpected package cannot be pulled silently.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique differs from installing a malicious file or image.
Describe typosquatting and dependency confusion as ways a bad package gets installed.
Explain why install time scripts make a package dangerous before it is ever used.
Identify build and package manager telemetry that reveals a malicious dependency.
Describe structural controls such as pinned versions, internal mirrors and provenance checks.
